items.summary: TL;DR: Financial institutions need to demonstrate that security controls are effective in production and that security investments reduce business risk. Across regulatory frameworks including NYDFS, OSFI, DORA, MAS and APRA, verified control evidence helps institutions demonstrate resilience and support accountable risk decisions. It replaced the original NIS Directive (EU) 2016/1148 and turned a loosely applied, sector-by-sector regime into a single framework with common obligations, common reporting timelines and real enforcement powers. So, what is NIS2 in practical terms for a security team? Three things. First, it defines who is in scope through size thresholds and two sector annexes, splitting covered organizations into essential and important entities. Second, it prescribes a minimum set of risk-management controls in Article 21, from incident handling and logging to supply chain security and cryptography. Third, it imposes a staged incident notification process in Article 23, with the first signal due to the national CSIRT or competent authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident. Because NIS2 is a directive rather than a regulation, every Member State writes its own national law. The core obligations are shared, but registration portals, supervisory authorities and reporting forms differ from Rome to Warsaw, which is exactly why a country-level view matters. Member States had until 17 October 2024 to transpose it, with national measures applying from 18 October 2024. Few made it: Italy and Belgium were among the handful that had laws in force on time. The Commission responded with letters of formal notice in November 2024, reasoned opinions in May 2025 and, on 8 July 2026, referrals to the Court of Justice of the EU for the remaining laggards. According to the nisd2.eu transposition tracker , as of 16 October 2026 a national law is in force in 24 of the 27 Member States. France, Ireland and Spain are still without one. For NIS2 compliance, the takeaway is that the clock is national, not European. Germany’s BSIG amendments have applied since 6 December 2025, Poland’s amended KSC Act since 3 April 2026, the Dutch Cyberbeveiligingswet since 15 August 2026 and Austria’s NISG 2026 since 1 October 2026. Each brings its own registration window, so a multi-country operator can be compliant in Milan while already late in Gdańsk. Management bodies must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures, oversee their implementation and complete regular training. Accountability no longer stops at the CISO. Technical controls sit in Article 21(2), which lists ten minimum measures: risk analysis and information system security policies; incident handling; business continuity, backup and crisis management; supply chain security; secure acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling; assessment of control effectiveness; cyber hygiene and training; cryptography; HR security, access control and asset management; and MFA plus secured communications. For digital infrastructure and ICT service providers, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 spells these out in detail, including explicit monitoring and logging requirements. Reporting sits in Article 23, and this is where SOC teams feel the pressure: 24 hours: early warning, including whether the incident is suspected to be malicious or to have cross-border impact 72 hours: incident notification with an initial severity and impact assessment and available indicators of compromise One month: final report with root cause, mitigation and cross-border impact A 24-hour early warning is only credible if the team can actually read its logs within hours, not days. Why the EU Replaced NIS1 with NIS2 NIS1 failed on consistency. Each Member State decided for itself which companies counted as operators of essential services, so two hospitals of the same size in neighbouring countries could face completely different obligations. Penalties were low and rarely applied, and incident reporting thresholds varied so widely that cross-border situational awareness barely existed. The threat picture moved faster than the law. Between the Commission’s December 2020 proposal and the final text, Europe saw ransomware take down hospital IT, the SolarWinds and Kaseya supply chain compromises reach thousands of downstream customers, and the February 2022 attack on Viasat’s KA-SAT network cut remote monitoring for around 5,800 Enercon wind turbines in Germany. It also formalises cooperation through EU-CyCLONe and the CSIRTs network, so a significant incident in Lyon is no longer a purely French problem. NIS2 Fines and Management Liability Article 34 sets the ceilings that national laws must reach at minimum: Entity type Maximum administrative fine Supervision model Essential At least €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Ex ante: audits, on-site inspections, security scans Important At least €7 million or 1.4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Ex post: triggered by evidence or an incident The turnover reference is the whole undertaking, not the local subsidiary, which is why group-level CFOs now read NIS2 briefings. Money is only part of the exposure. For essential entities, Article 32 allows authorities to suspend certifications or authorisations and to temporarily bar a CEO or legal representative from managerial functions until deficiencies are fixed. Authorities can also order an entity to publicly disclose its non-compliance. In practice, regulators look for evidence. An organization that can show when it detected an incident, which logs it examined and how it reached its 24-hour and 72-hour conclusions is in a far stronger position than one that reconstructs the timeline after the fact. Documented, repeatable log analysis is the cheapest insurance against the upper end of these penalties. NIS2 vs. DORA: Which One Applies? A one-line NIS2 directive summary: horizontal cybersecurity rules for 18 critical sectors, transposed nationally. DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), is the opposite on both counts. It is sector-specific, covering banks, insurers, investment firms, payment institutions, crypto-asset service providers and their critical ICT third-party providers, and as a regulation it has applied directly in every Member State since 17 January 2025. The two connect through Article 4 of NIS2. Where a sector-specific EU act imposes requirements at least equivalent to NIS2, that act prevails. DORA is that lex specialis for financial entities, so a bank follows DORA’s ICT risk, testing and reporting rules rather than the NIS2 versions. A managed SOC or cloud provider can be an important entity under NIS2 and, at the same time, a contractual ICT provider under DORA, facing two sets of log evidence requests. Under NIS2, it is a significant incident affecting service delivery, reported to the CSIRT or competent authority starting at 24 hours, whether or not any personal data was touched. A ransomware attack on a hospital usually triggers both. Article 35 of NIS2 requires the cybersecurity authority to inform the data protection authority when an incident may involve a personal data breach, and it prevents a double fine for the same conduct where a GDPR penalty has already been imposed. Annex I, sectors of high criticality (11): energy, transport, banking, financial market infrastructure, health, drinking water, waste water, digital infrastructure, B2B ICT service management, public administration and space. Annex II, other critical sectors (7): postal and courier services, waste management, chemicals, food production and distribution, manufacturing (medical devices, electronics, electrical equipment, machinery, motor vehicles and other transport equipment), digital providers and research. items.title: How to keep your architecture intact when agents write the code
items.summary: AI agents are generating code at a pace that far outstrips any human's ability to review it. That shift moves the engineer’s job upward, away from typing lines in an IDE to governing overall structure. Agents can write a working function, but the bigger issue is whether the system that function joins still holds together six months from now. Matt Erman, Senior Software Engineer at Blackboard and author of the Manning book “Grokking Software Architecture,” joined Tom Howlett on episode 6 of The Next Commit. The discussion centered around a problem Matt has been working on from the architect's chair. His conclusion: the fundamentals of good software engineering still hold, but the way teams practice them has to change. What follows is his playbook for keeping architecture intact while agents scale output, and why verification has to carry the load that human review no longer can. Why an agent's intelligence is the problem, not the solution The common complaint about coding agents is that they are dumb. Matt turned this notion on its head, saying "[part] of the problem with AI agents is that they're too smart," and continued, "They know the entire internet. Everything that you could possibly know about architecture, the AI agent can know or knows." That breadth is exactly the risk. An agent with every architectural pattern in its training data, handed a vague task, will reach for all of them at once. "If you don't constrain it, it will essentially take a hodgepodge of all these different architectures or ideas and patterns and just mix them together," Matt said, "because it doesn't know what you're actually trying to accomplish." Most engineering organizations adopting AI tooling have discovered a powerful structural insight: constraint is actually the key to success. The more you narrow the solution space with architectural boundaries, the more an agent's knowledge becomes an asset instead of a source of entropy. "The more you can constrain it architecturally, the more you can constrain it with boundaries, the better your results are gonna be," Matt said, "because it won't allow the agent to go outside of those. Or if it does, it will fail the build and the agent will have to retry it." Human review cannot scale, so stop trying to scale it From Matt’s perspective, human code review has hit a wall. "AI agents are putting out so much code that human review is becoming almost impossible because you can't scale it," he said. "Even if you had ten people reviewing the code, all they'd be doing is reviewing code and not doing anything else." Add more reviewers and you add more failure modes. People get tired. They take vacation. They have a bad day and rubber-stamp a diff they should have questioned. Multiply that across the volume agents now generate, and human review becomes the weakest link in the system. Matt’s answer to these challenges is a shift in where you invest. "You don't optimize the code, you optimize the feedback loop," Matt said. "You basically scale the verification process around the agent instead of scaling the manual review process. Because that's what ultimately we'll be able to scale." The safety net shifts from human attention to automated, independent code verification . The loop runs the same way every time, at machine speed, across every change. It catches what a distracted reviewer misses, and it does not get tired. Fitness functions: the mechanism that holds architecture in place The load-bearing piece of Matt's verification layer is architectural fitness functions. They test something unit and integration tests cannot reach: the structural rules of the system itself. "You can write all the unit tests you want," Matt said. "Those will check your code... but they don’t necessarily check the architectural bounds." A fitness function does. It verifies that a controller stays clean, that a component respects its dependency direction, that nothing reaches into the database when it should go through the proper service. The reason this matters is cost. An architectural violation might not cause any visible problem for months. Then it compounds. "Over the course of time, your architecture continues to degrade until you hit a point where it just fails completely," Matt said. "When that happens, that becomes much more expensive to fix than fixing a random code bug, because those are foundational components that need to be redone and re-architected." A bug has a small blast radius, whereas architectural rot can take down the whole application. Fitness functions earn their keep twice. After implementation, they reject violations and force the agent to retry the right way. Before implementation, they act as an executable specification. Matt bakes them into the engineering guidelines his agent reads before planning, which also describe the target architecture. “So when it designs the plan, it already has [everything] planned out based on how the architecture should look." The agent arrives at the plan already constrained, so it rarely goes off track in the first place. When something does escape, Matt fixes it and then locks it down. "The one thing that is extremely important is that you not only fix it, but you also create regression tests around it," Matt said. Each defect that slips through becomes a regression test, a durable record that both the team and the agent can learn from. items.summary: Gemini 4 Argon passes 85.66% of the tasks it is tested on. In our evaluation, it also produces more blocker vulnerabilities than blocker bugs. Passing tests and being safe to ship are different questions, and this model shows the gap clearly. Most of its findings are maintainability issues. Most of its severe findings are security issues. How was Gemini 4 Argon evaluated? Model: Gemini 4 Argon, high reasoning effort Language: Java Benchmark: the same Java benchmark we use for every model, covering HumanEval, MBPP and ComplexCodeEval. The run records 4,444 tasks. All of them are analyzed for code quality and security, which is where every density figure below comes from. Of those, 544 of them ship with executable tests, and the pass rate covers only those. Analyzer: SonarQube systematic code analysis. Complexity and code smell densities are per 1,000 lines of code (kLOC). Bug and vulnerability densities, and all category breakdowns, are per million lines (mLOC). Three terms worth defining first: Cyclomatic complexity: counts independent paths through a function. Cognitive complexity: a SonarQube metric that weights nested and deeply branched logic more heavily, reflecting how hard the code is for a human to read. Severity: the impact level a finding carries, inherited from the rule that raised it. It describes how much a finding affects the software qualities Sonar measures. It is not a prediction of how likely that code is to reach production. Gemini 4 Argon key metrics at a glance Metric Gemini 4 Argon Lines of code (total) 619,852 Functions 85,245 Comments density (% of LOC) 4.6% Cyclomatic complexity per kLOC 244.39 Cognitive complexity per kLOC 148.97 Bugs 347 Vulnerabilities 193 Code smells 9,626 All findings 10,166 Overall issue density per kLOC 16.40 Functional skill (pass rate) 85.66% Missing completions 1.55% What is Gemini 4 Argon's functional pass rate? Of all 4,444 tasks, 69 returned no usable code at all, which is 1.55%. That matters because 33 of them fall inside the 544 test-backed tasks, the same set the pass rate is drawn from. A task with no completion produces nothing to analyze and nothing to run, so it is not a failed attempt so much as an absent one. If you are planning around this model, treat the pass rate and the completion rate as two separate questions. How much code does Gemini 4 Argon generate? Gemini 4 Argon generated 619,852 lines across the benchmark, spread over 85,245 functions and 22,656 classes. That function count is the number to notice. It works out at 7.3 lines per function and about 3 statements each, with roughly 27 lines per class. This is code built from many small pieces rather than a few large ones. Fine-grained functions are generally easier to read and test one at a time. The trade is that following a single operation can mean moving through more of them, so reviewers spend more time on call paths and less on any individual body. Comment lines total 30,029, which is 4.6% of output. There is a reasonable amount of inline context for anyone picking the code up later. How complex is Gemini 4 Argon's generated code? Cyclomatic complexity is 244.39 per kLOC and cognitive complexity is 148.97 per kLOC. Read those two together rather than separately. Cyclomatic counts decision points. Cognitive weights the nested ones more heavily. Cognitive sitting well below cyclomatic says the branching is frequent but mostly flat, so there are many decisions and comparatively little logic buried inside other logic. Combined with 7.3 lines per function, that is a consistent picture: short functions, plenty of branches, shallow nesting. Neither figure tells you whether the code works, but both indicate how much a reviewer has to hold in their head at once, and shallow beats deep on that measure. For a team triaging reliability work, most of it sits in the tier that wants fixing without stopping the release. The largest, concurrency and threading, is 58 findings, or 17% of the total. The next six all land between 34 and 57. Seven categories therefore cover 319 of the 347 bugs with no single one carrying the group. The consequence is that there is no single lever for bug remediation here. A team that fixes every concurrency finding has cleared 17% of the reliability work and left six other categories largely untouched. Concurrency findings still deserve attention disproportionate to their count. They are among the harder bugs to catch in review and to reproduce once they ship, because they depend on timing and on the environment they run in. Maintainability severity Per mLOC BLOCKER 58 CRITICAL 2,691 MAJOR 6,321 MINOR 5,814 INFO 645 Major and minor carry 7,522 of the 9,626 findings between them, and blocker is 36. Code smell category Per mLOC Collection / generics parameter type 3,896 Design / framework best practices 2,559 Regex / pattern / string format 1,881 Cognitive computational complexity 1,721 Naming / style / documentation 1,497 Dead / unused / redundant code 1,366 Assignment / field / scope visibility 1,144 Control / conditional logic 994 Deprecation / obsolete API 329 Uncategorized 137 Structure / architecture 5 Collection and generics is the largest category at 25% of all smells. That row spans raw types and missing type parameters, redundant casts, and collection handling that could be simpler, so the total does not tell you how much of it is any one of those. How many tokens does Gemini 4 Argon use? Tokens Gemini 4 Argon Input 1,517,336 Output 6,362,719 Reasoning 11,886,018 Total 19,766,073 One accounting note before reading these. In this run, reasoning tokens are reported separately from output tokens rather than inside them, and the three figures add to the total. Not every provider reports it this way, so this is not a number to set against a reasoning figure from another model without checking first. The headline is the ratio. Gemini 4 Argon spent 11.9 million tokens reasoning and 6.4 million producing code, which is about 1.9 thinking tokens for every token written. Reasoning alone is 60% of the total spend. Per line of generated Java that works out at roughly 10 output tokens and 19 reasoning tokens. This is a model that deliberates, which is consistent with the high reasoning effort setting this run used. If you are budgeting for it, the reasoning side is the larger line item by a wide margin. There are 22 blocker vulnerabilities and 132 critical ones, in a group that is under 2% of all findings. Two categories hold two thirds of it, and both are well covered by automated analysis, so of the three risks here this is the one that narrows down cleanly. The spread of the bugs is second. Vulnerabilities are 1.9% of them, but 80% of those are blocker or critical, against 12% of bugs and 18% of code smells. Bug remediation has no single lever. The largest bug category is 17% of the total, and seven categories are all roughly the same size. Reliability review has to stay broad. It spends more on reasoning than on writing. It used 11.9 million reasoning tokens against 6.4 million output tokens, and 19.8 million in total. The total is about two and a half times the GPT-6 runs we have published, which used medium effort where this run used high. If you are estimating spend, start from the reasoning figure rather than the amount of code you expect back. What to do next If you adopt Gemini 4 Argon, point automated checks at cryptography misconfiguration and insecure resource handling first. Together they hold two thirds of its security findings. SonarQube flags the first two through algorithmic analysis on every change, at the speed the model writes code. One caveat on reading any row in this table: each category groups a lot of rules, 17 Java rules in the case of collection and generics, and they are not all the same kind of problem. That row spans raw types and missing type parameters, redundant casts, and collection handling that could be simpler, so the total does not tell you how much of it is any one of those.

How many tokens does Gemini 4 Argon use?

Tokens

Gemini 4 Argon

Input

1,517,336

Output

6,362,719

Reasoning

11,886,018

Total

19,766,073

One accounting note before reading these. In this run, reasoning tokens are reported separately from output tokens rather than inside them, and the three figures add to the total. Not every provider reports it this way, so this is not a number to set against a reasoning figure from another model without checking first.

The headline is the ratio. Gemini 4 Argon spent 11.9 million tokens reasoning and 6.4 million producing code, which is about 1.9 thinking tokens for every token written. Reasoning alone is 60% of the total spend.

Per line of generated Java that works out at roughly 10 output tokens and 19 reasoning tokens. This is a model that deliberates, which is consistent with the high reasoning effort setting this run used. If you are budgeting for it, the reasoning side is the larger line item by a wide margin.

What are the biggest risks of using Gemini 4 Argon-generated code in production?

Three places to point verification effort.

Security is first, and it is first by severity rather than by volume. There are 22 blocker vulnerabilities and 132 critical ones, in a group that is under 2% of all findings. Two categories hold two thirds of it, and both are well covered by automated analysis, so of the three risks here this is the one that narrows down cleanly.

The spread of the bugs is second. With 347 bugs spread across seven categories of  roughly the same size, reliability review cannot be narrowed to one or two rule groups. Clearing the largest category, concurrency, addresses 58 findings and leaves 289. Plan for breadth.

Missing completions are third. In total, 69 tasks returned nothing, and 33 of those sit in the test-backed subset. This is not a code quality measure at all, which is exactly why it is easy to miss. A task that produces no code produces no findings and no test result, so it looks clean in every table in this article.

Three takeaways:

  • Most findings are maintainability issues. Security findings are the most severe. Code smells are 95% of the 10,166 findings. Vulnerabilities are 1.9% of them, but 80% of those are blocker or critical, against 12% of bugs and 18% of code smells.
  • Bug remediation has no single lever. The largest bug category is 17% of the total, and seven categories are all roughly the same size. Reliability review has to stay broad.
  • It spends more on reasoning than on writing. It used 11.9 million reasoning tokens against 6.4 million output tokens, and 19.8 million in total. The total is about two and a half times the GPT-6 runs we have published, which used medium effort where this run used high. If you are estimating spend, start from the reasoning figure rather than the amount of code you expect back.

What to do next

If you adopt Gemini 4 Argon, point automated checks at cryptography misconfiguration and insecure resource handling first. Together they hold two thirds of its security findings. Keep reliability review broad, because no single bug category carries the load. And track missing completions separately, because a task that returns no code never shows up as a finding. SonarQube flags the first two through algorithmic analysis on every change, at the speed the model writes code.

items.title: Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
items.summary: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain . Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. Performance and memory improvements Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers: As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs , and we’re hoping to find more. You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration. By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster: Try tsrs TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm: npm install tsrs npx tsrs Why now? We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go. However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript. Why Rust? You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?” However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly . The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency. Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before. This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application. How will the tsrs port be maintained? First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post : Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix. We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins. Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release. What’s next? Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint. Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc . We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

items.title: Google may add your number to all your accounts: How to stop it
items.summary: As Android Central reports , users have received unexpected emails telling them their phone number has been verified for secondary Google accounts. Like me and many others, you may have one Google account for everyday use, another for work, and a third for things you would rather keep separate. But if you’re using an Android phone, those accounts may have something in common that you didn’t intend or even know about: your phone number. Google’s own documentation confirms that phone number verification is on by default and adds your number to all Google accounts signed in on the device. This applies to both existing accounts and any you add later. Google says phone number verification helps support features such as signing in, account recovery, Rich Communications Services (RCS) messaging, and finding or securing a lost device. But it also means that a number you intended to use with your main account can become associated with a secondary account simply because both are signed in on the same Android device. If you deliberately left your phone number off a secondary account, this links it to your real identity without you knowingly making that connection. Your number doesn’t automatically become public, but Google gains another way to connect accounts you wanted to keep separate. This reminded me of an article I wrote about unexpected Google account connections: “ Google Play sign-ins can be abused to track another person’s movements .” Signing in to Google Play on one phone allowed me to see its movements in Google Maps Timeline. “After some digging I learned that my Google account was added to my wife’s phone’s accounts when I logged in on the Play Store, but was not removed when I logged out after noticing the tracking issue.” While that particular issue should be solved by Google’s move toward device-based Timeline storage, unwanted phone number associations need to be removed manually. How to remove your number from separate accounts Phone manufacturers arrange their settings differently, so there may be some differences in menu names and locations. We tried to make sure everyone can follow these instructions, but there might be makes and models where you get stuck. Feel free to ask in the comments and maybe others with the same phone can help you. Step 1: Turn off automatic phone number verification This needs to be done on the Android phone itself: Open the phone’s Settings app. Tap Google . On some phones, this may be called Google services or Google services and preferences . Open All services . Under Privacy & security , tap Phone number verification . Turn off Verify phone numbers automatically , or the equivalent verification switch shown on your phone. Turning this off does not remove numbers already added to your accounts. Step 2: Check which accounts already have your number This step can be done in a browser, so should be the same for everyone. Open a browser and type myaccount.google.com into the address bar. Check the account picture or initial in the top-right corner. Make sure you are looking at the account you want to inspect. Select Personal info . Find Contact info , then select Phone . Depending on the layout, you may see Phone directly. Select any number listed to review its details and how it is used. To remove the number from that account, select the delete icon and follow the on-screen instructions. Repeat for each account you want to check. Step 3: Check for other uses of the number There’s a wrinkle. Google says changing a number in your Google Account only affects some services. Other services, such as 2-Step Verification , may use the number separately and may not all appear on the Phone page. On each account you are cleaning up: Check the number’s Usage section on the Phone page to see which services are listed. Visit Security or Security & sign-in and review your recovery phone and 2-Step Verification settings. If you use another Google service that has its own phone number settings, check those settings too. If your goal is to remove the number entirely from a particular account, don’t assume deleting it from Personal info has removed every separate use. Check those security settings as well, but make sure to keep a working alternative sign-in and recovery method before removing the number. items.title: CVE-2026-110936: Siemens Software Center Flaw Exploited in ClickFix Attacks
items.summary: Siemens has confirmed active exploitation of a high-severity DLL side-loading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center, a desktop application used to download, install, activate, and update Siemens software. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936 and rated 8.4 under CVSS v4.0, the flaw stems from an uncontrolled DLL search path and can lead to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application. The vulnerability has already been weaponized in ClickFix activity linked by Siemens to the Romulus delivery platform. In observed attacks, threat actors paired a legitimate, digitally signed copy of Siemens Software Center with attacker-controlled DLL files rather than modifying the Siemens executable itself. Siemens stressed that its systems, products, and official update channels were not breached. Security teams looking for CVE-2026-110936 detection content can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation, DLL side-loading, suspicious process execution, and related post-compromise behavior. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunt for emerging malicious activity. To Detect CVE-2026-110936 exploitation and related attack patterns, defenders should prioritize behavior-based analytics instead of relying exclusively on hashes of the signed Siemens executable. SOC Prime detections can be applied across multiple SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake technologies and aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK® framework. Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect and Uncoder AI capabilities to transform fresh threat intelligence and indicators into hunting queries, refine detection logic, and accelerate detection engineering workflows. Contact Sales CVE-2026-110936 Analysis CVE-2026-110936 affects Siemens Software Center versions earlier than 4.0.9.8. Siemens classifies the vulnerability as CWE-427, Uncontrolled Search Path Element. The affected application can search an insufficiently restricted location for DLL files, potentially allowing an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted library in a searched directory and execute code with the privileges of Siemens Software Center. The active campaign demonstrates how this weakness can be incorporated into a social-engineering-driven malware chain. Attackers distributed a genuine Siemens Software Center executable carrying a valid digital signature together with malicious DLL files. Siemens said version 3.5.8.7, the latest release at the time of the observed attacks, loaded helper files located alongside the executable without validating them first. As a result, the legitimate Siemens executable itself was not modified. Instead, malicious functionality resided inside attacker-supplied DLL files that were loaded when Software Center started. This approach lets adversaries abuse the trust associated with a legitimately signed application while executing attacker-controlled code. The Hacker News reports that the attack chain used msiexec.exe to launch AllMyBasic.msi, which subsequently executed SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe. Siemens identified archive.dll as one of the malicious components associated with the campaign. Siemens has attributed the activity to Romulus, a multi-platform ClickFix delivery operation. ClickFix attacks typically present victims with deceptive prompts, such as fake CAPTCHA or verification instructions, that persuade users to copy and execute malicious commands themselves. Related Romulus activity has also been observed delivering LegionLoader and abusing legitimate signed applications from other vendors for DLL side-loading. items.title: ownCloud at OSS EU 2026 and Why Community Matters
items.summary: Why community engagement is so important We had the privilege of joining the Linux Foundation’s Open Source Summit Europe in Prague earlier this month (7 to 9 October) as a sponsor. First, a big thank you to everyone involved for a wonderful experience! We also weren’t alone. The booth was staffed by a mix of folks from ownCloud and Kiteworks, plus people from our partners Collabora , B1 Systems and Cesnet . Having everyone in one place meant almost any question, from “how do I run this at home” to “how would this fit our infrastructure”, could be answered by someone who actually works with it every day. Our main goals were to re-engage with the community, (re-)introduce people to oCIS and ownCloud, and to listen. And oh boy, were we not disappointed. “I thought you were dead!” and “I’m so glad you’re still here!” were some of the things we most often heard from folks at the conferences and meetups we’ve attended this year, which makes sense, because unfortunately we dropped the ball in community engagement since the end of 2024, and we’ve apologized to the community and our partners for it. We let people down and working in a seemingly black box is the opposite of what Open Source stands for. So, for the record: yes, we’re still alive. But “not dead” is a pretty low bar, and being back in the same room as you reminded me why I fell for open source in the first place. But it only works well when people show up, talk to each other, and occasionally tell you you’re doing it wrong. (We got a bit of all three – and we sincerely thank you for that!) Here’s how the week went, starting a day before the summit with a room full of fellow OSPO nerds – and I say that with love. Starting with OSPOlogy Our week actually started the day before the summit, at OpenChain x OSPOlogy Prague . It was a full-day community event for people who work on open source management, supply chain trust and OSPOs, and it was a great fit for us. We launched the Kiteworks/ownCloud Open Source Program Office (OSPO) earlier this year, so it felt like being among our own people. David Walter, who leads our OSPO, gave a session there called “Two Forks and a CLA-to-DCO Rewrite: What Actually Rebuilds Community Trust”. Honest conversations about forks, governance and trust are rarely comfortable, but they’re the ones that matter most for a project with our history. We enjoyed the rest of the day just as much. Nithya Ruff’s keynote on OSPOs and open technology was a highlight, and so were the hands-on sessions. Dawn Foster’s roundtable on improving your OSPO with CHAOSS made the case for “strategy before metrics”, and one theme stuck with me: metrics need a narrator, because the same dashboard can lead two people to completely different conclusions. Ana Jiménez’s demo on using AI agents with CHAOSS security metrics gave us an interesting look into how she built AI tooling geared towards OSPOs. If you missed it, the presentations and roundtable notes are collected in the OSPOlogy GitHub discussion (because of course they’re open – the day was centered around OSPOs and our love of Open Source!) What we learned A lot of people think we’re a cloud hosting company. Given the name, that’s understandable, and we heard it often enough that eventually we stopped being surprised. Many people assumed we’d try to sell them a public cloud service and we need to fix that. One idea I’m toying with is a tagline like “Bring your own storage, create your ownCloud”. Nothing is final, so tell me what you think. Most people know ownCloud Classic, the PHP version. Plenty of folks were still running it in their homelabs and were happy to find out the project is alive. Somewhere out there is a quietly humming box in a closet that has been faithfully syncing files this whole time, and I love that. But most of them had no idea oCIS exists – another thing to work on. oCIS is fully open source written in Go, with no gated features. This is the one that surprised people most. ownCloud Classic followed an open-core model, so many people assumed oCIS would too. It doesn’t and everything is open and not gated. This is definitely something we need to put front and center, because this was the selling point for a lot of folks. (The fact that it is cloud-native and doesn’t need a database to run, also left quite a few people eager to try it) People were willing to try it. Many of those who hadn’t heard of oCIS were keen to spin it up and try it out. That was probably the most encouraging part of the week. (You can use the same ownCloud demo site we used to try out ownCloud and Collabora right now) People want to know what’s coming. Questions about the future of ownCloud Classic, where oCIS is headed, and where to find the public roadmap came up a lot. That’s fair, and it’s an area where we can and want to be more transparent. Lean or robust, your call One question came up a lot: how big is this thing, really? oCIS is as lean as you want it to be, or as robust as you need. Its modular, extension-based architecture keeps the core simple, so a small setup stays small and an enterprise can build up from there without the core getting complicated. Think of it as a very well-organized toolbox rather than a Swiss Army knife that never closes properly. That’s deliberate. ownCloud focuses on file sync and share, and we’d rather pair that with best-in-class integrations (document editing with Collabora is a good example) than try to build everything ourselves. Doing one thing well, and playing nicely with others who do the same, is pretty much the open source spirit. If you want to see how the extension side works, we wrote about the new ownCloud Marketplace, where Git is the app store . “So what’s your business model?” Once people hear that nothing is gated, the next question is almost always the same, and I love it. If the software is fully open, how does this work? The project itself is not productized. Rather we have funding through organizations that need enterprise-level support that we maintain and build the features they need, which then land in the open codebase for everybody. These are ongoing contracts from the ownCloud Classic era who have now migrated to oCIS. Kiteworks also backs the project as a corporate sponsor (they are our parent company now after all). For people with needs we can’t serve directly, we point to our partner ecosystem, which is one more reason we were so glad to have partners like Collabora, B1 Systems and Cesnet at the booth. There’s a bigger reason I care about this, too: digital sovereignty. With an open license, organizations know the code can outlive any single vendor, whatever happens to that vendor. For a lot of people we know that matters a lot. If you want the longer story of how we got here (the forks, the acquisition, and what we’re changing), I covered it in my FrOSCon talk, Bringing back the Open in Open Source: (Re-)Building Community after forks and acquisition . It’s a case study, and not always a flattering one (and that’s maybe the point). ownCloud Contribution spotlight Contributing doesn’t mean only writing code. Documentation, tutorials, extensions, forum help, bug reports and feature requests all count, and you can bundle several smaller contributions into one entry (a lone typo fix is lovely, but it won’t make the spotlight on its own. Typo fixers, we still love you). The ownCloud Contribution Spotlight is our way of saying thank you to the people who make ownCloud better. Entries for The Launch edition are open until December 1 and we’ll announce the winner at the Monthly Public Community Sprint review on December 18 who gets a ticket to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2027 in Barcelona. Afterwards, from January 2027, this will be a program where we feature and reward a new contribution/contributor every month. If you’ve contributed, or you know someone who has, join in. Highlights from the team For all of us, the best part was getting to interact with the community: hearing how people use ownCloud, what they want more of, and what they honestly think of the company and the product. The keynote conversation between Linus Torvalds and Dirk Hohndel on the last morning was also great, as was the OSPOlogy day. A few other things the team took away: The event felt community driven, not sales driven. Nobody was trying to push a subscription, and if someone wanted help with their own setup, they could get it right at the booth. Some of us were surprised by how many people already know ownCloud. It’s good to see how well the project is regarded in the open source world. Talking with customers and partners left the team convinced that investing in open source is the right call. Explaining things to others is a very efficient way to learn them. Some of us arrived knowing less about ownCloud than we do now. Most visitors seemed genuinely interested in talking to the people behind the products. Long days on your feet at a booth are exhausting, though we get better prepared each time. (Comfortable shoes: the real open source infrastructure.) And one more thank you, because it deserves its own line: Thank you to the Linux Foundation, the events team and all the volunteers for a great event and a wonderful sponsor experience. Everything ran smoothly, and the people we met were great. Come join us If we met in Prague, thank you. You reminded us why we do this. If we didn’t, there’s still a seat for you, and here’s how to grab it: Subscribe to our community newsletter: com/community-events/#newsletter Join the community at owncloud.com Try out a demo of ownCloud and Collabora : owncloud.com Join our monthly public community reviews , where we share what’s happening and listen to what you want next: com/community-events Join the contribution spotlight and let us thank you properly: read how it works Learn more about how the Kiteworks/ownCloud OSPO approaches open source: kiteworks.com/open-source Open source is only as strong as the people who show up for it. Come show up and engage with us.

items.title: Hackers Hijack 790 GitHub Repositories to Steal Cloud Credentials and AI API Keys
items.summary: A campaign called GhostAction has placed malicious GitHub Actions workflows in 790 repositories, putting cloud credentials, software-publishing tokens, and AI service keys at risk. The total is OpenSourceMalware’s count of publicly recoverable, validated repositories through October 9, 2026; it is not a claim that every repository leaked credentials or suffered confirmed misuse. The campaign abuses trusted developer accounts. Once an attacker can write to a maintainer’s repositories, they can add a workflow that runs when code is pushed or when someone starts it manually. This can expose secrets available to the workflow, turning a stolen account into a route toward cloud systems, package registries, and other projects. Researchers from OpenSourceMalware identified this latest stage while investigating a malicious PyPI package called claudecord and helping its maintainer respond. Revolut’s status page listed 28 services as partially unavailable, including account sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading and live support chat. Reuters also reported disruption to ATM withdrawals. For customers, that meant problems could extend beyond opening the app. An affected card payment could interrupt a purchase, while unavailable transfers or cash withdrawals could limit access to funds. Disruption to support chat also affected a channel customers would normally use to ask about payment failures or account access. “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” Revolut said. The company added that it had been working to fix the issue since identifying it that morning and apologized to affected customers. The reported connection to Google Cloud places the focus on service availability and cloud dependencies. Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI, Then Accidentally Expose Their Own Attack Tools
items.summary: Hackers linked to AI-assisted attacks on South Korean banks left parts of their own infrastructure open, giving researchers a view of their tools and preparations. The exposed files showed a wider operation involving cryptocurrency theft tools, Linux attacks, and mobile security testing beyond the banking campaign. Public reporting cited in the investigation said the breaches exposed personal information belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions. Different organizations lost different types of data, including customer records and an outsourced developer’s personal details, rather than suffering one identical breach. Researchers from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the attack tools while investigating infrastructure linked to the actor, tracked as TAG-217. Their October 16 research report traced preparations back to August 2026. It described scripts and capabilities, not a newly named malware family, and showed how basic security mistakes exposed the operator’s work. Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI The campaign involved ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source framework for penetration testing. Such tools help authorized security teams find weaknesses, but attackers can use them against targets without permission. Earlier reporting on the AI-assisted bank breach campaign described exposed Claude Code sessions, ARTEX settings, and AI memory files that helped reveal the operator’s workflow. Public analysis dated October 7 linked the activity to Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Investigators suspected a Chinese-speaking operator, but language clues do not establish nationality or government backing. Recorded Future assessed that the broader activity likely reflected attempts to make money across several possible targets. The incidents also drew attention to systems outside core banking services. Network Infrastructure (Source – Recorded Future) Reporting on the South Korean security investigation described breaches affecting loan-agent and employee-support systems, showing why security reviews must cover connected business applications as well as customer banking platforms. These supporting services can still hold valuable personal and credit information. Exposed Files Reveal Earlier Preparations Open directories and other exposed evidence allowed Insikt Group to reconstruct activity from August 17–22. During that period, TAG-217 tested infrastructure for maintaining remote access and scanned internet-facing systems. Logs showed repeated connections between the actor’s own servers, but did not establish successful access to victims. By August 22, the operator had assembled tools targeting cryptocurrency mining operations using YiiMP. Their functions included trying default passwords, stealing wallet configuration and key files, keeping remote access, and sending Telegram alerts when credentials were captured. Other tools targeted known Linux weaknesses to gain higher access or extract protected password data. By September 5, the workspace included experiments involving iPhone weaknesses and changes to Android system software. Again, the available logs showed testing, not confirmed mobile compromises. By September 26, records covered target research, traffic routing, payload delivery, and checks involving payment processes, revealing a broader toolkit than the banking attacks alone suggested. TAG-217 also routed traffic through residential internet connections, likely to hide its source. As reporting on residential proxy network abuse explains, these services make traffic appear to come from ordinary household connections. The operator also maintained links between servers and copied AI working-memory files across its infrastructure. The exposed material demonstrates AI use, but it does not measure how much AI accelerated the attacks or prove that an autonomous agent completed every intrusion. Recorded Future emphasized this limit: the evidence shows the range of environments explored, rather than a confirmed success against every target represented in the toolkit. For defenders, the lesson is practical. Review internet-facing employee and partner applications, fix exposed weaknesses, and check that users can retrieve only authorized records. Monitor unusual sign-ins, repeated customer-record requests, unexpected remote access, and abnormal data transfers. Response automation should use clear approval limits, especially when blocking shared proxy addresses could affect legitimate customers. items.title: ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform That Uses Multiple Hacking Agents to Find Security Flaws
items.summary: ThreatBook has launched RedAgents, a cloud platform that brings several AI-powered penetration-testing agents together to assess an organization’s systems. Announced on October 16, 2026, the service is designed to help security teams find weaknesses in their own networks by running multiple automated tests within a defined, authorized scope. ThreatBook says the agents can work in parallel and show their findings and test logs in one place. The platform takes a different approach from relying on a single testing tool or provider. Each agent may look for different issues, so combining their results could give defenders a broader view of their exposure. The launch announcement describes RedAgents as a software-as-a-service platform for security operations teams, rather than a new malware family or a report on a specific intrusion. ThreatBook’s announcement also notes that the service brings together agents with different origins and capabilities. Those named at launch are Artex Pro, Cyber(YanJi), Yanxun and CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition. The company says teams can choose one agent or run several against the same approved target, then review results through a shared interface. ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform RedAgents acts as an aggregator: it connects multiple AI penetration-testing agents through one platform and can run them in parallel. A penetration test is an authorized review in which testers look for weaknesses in systems before malicious actors can exploit them. Running agents side by side may help uncover issues that a single tool misses, though the value of the results depends on how accurately the agents test and report. ThreatBook says the platform consolidates findings, test data and logs in a unified view. This could reduce the need for teams to move information between separate tools. The approach is similar to using multiple scanners or testing teams, but RedAgents is designed to coordinate AI agents as part of one assessment. For readers comparing different designs, Cybersecurity News has covered a multi-agent pentesting toolkit that assigns different testing tasks to specialist agents. The four named agents have distinct backgrounds. ThreatBook describes Artex Pro as the enterprise version of Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing agent. Cyber(YanJi) is a Python-based agent that searches for a route from a starting point to a defined goal. Yanxun is described as a system that coordinates specialist agents, while CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition is based on an AI-native testing tool that ThreatBook acquired in September 2026. These descriptions come from the company’s announcement and should be read as vendor claims, not as independent comparative test results. ThreatBook reports, for example, that Yanxun can coordinate several dozen agents and that Cyber(YanJi) solved 54 of 54 challenge problems during a validation event. The release does not provide a controlled, side-by-side benchmark showing how all four agents perform against the same targets. Scope and data controls Automated testing tools can cause disruption if they probe systems without permission or exceed an agreed scope. ThreatBook says RedAgents lets customers define an allowlist of approved targets and that agents must operate within those authorized limits. Organizations should still confirm the scope, timing, rate limits and test conditions before running any penetration test, especially on systems that support business operations. The company also says customer test data stays within the ThreatBook environment and is not sent to third-party agents. RedAgents supports Zero Data Retention, or ZDR, which ThreatBook says enables complete deletion of test data. Security teams should confirm how these controls work in practice, including retention periods, access permissions, logging and any contractual terms, before submitting sensitive environment details. The launch comes as more security products use AI agents to automate parts of testing. Other examples covered by Cybersecurity News include PentestCode’s AI testing agent and Xalgorix’s verification-focused platform . These products differ in how they are deployed and how they handle findings, so teams should compare scope controls, evidence quality and data handling rather than treating “AI pentesting” as one uniform category. The main promise of RedAgents is breadth: multiple agents may explore a target in different ways and give teams a combined view of possible weaknesses. That does not guarantee that every result is valid or that every vulnerability will be found. Security staff still need to review evidence, reproduce important findings safely and prioritize fixes based on business impact and exposure. ThreatBook says the platform can reduce false positives by combining agent results, but the announcement does not publish independent accuracy figures or a false-positive rate. It also does not identify a specific customer deployment, measured security outcome or external validation of the service. Those details will matter to organizations assessing whether the platform fits their testing process. For context, a separate Cybersecurity News report describes Apex’s black-box testing approach , which evaluates applications without source-code access. RedAgents’ stated distinction is not a single testing method but a central platform for selecting and coordinating several agents. ThreatBook says it plans to add more open-source agents over time, alongside the enterprise tools available at launch. The company’s announcement and RedAgents product blog provide further product details. RedAgents is available through the company’s website, where ThreatBook says organizations can request a trial. Running agents side by side may help uncover issues that a single tool misses, though the value of the results depends on how accurately the agents test and report.

ThreatBook says the platform consolidates findings, test data and logs in a unified view. This could reduce the need for teams to move information between separate tools.

The approach is similar to using multiple scanners or testing teams, but RedAgents is designed to coordinate AI agents as part of one assessment.

For readers comparing different designs, Cybersecurity News has covered a multi-agent pentesting toolkit that assigns different testing tasks to specialist agents.

The four named agents have distinct backgrounds. ThreatBook describes Artex Pro as the enterprise version of Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing agent. Cyber(YanJi) is a Python-based agent that searches for a route from a starting point to a defined goal.

Yanxun is described as a system that coordinates specialist agents, while CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition is based on an AI-native testing tool that ThreatBook acquired in September 2026.

These descriptions come from the company’s announcement and should be read as vendor claims, not as independent comparative test results.

ThreatBook reports, for example, that Yanxun can coordinate several dozen agents and that Cyber(YanJi) solved 54 of 54 challenge problems during a validation event.

The release does not provide a controlled, side-by-side benchmark showing how all four agents perform against the same targets.

Scope and data controls

Automated testing tools can cause disruption if they probe systems without permission or exceed an agreed scope. ThreatBook says RedAgents lets customers define an allowlist of approved targets and that agents must operate within those authorized limits.

Organizations should still confirm the scope, timing, rate limits and test conditions before running any penetration test, especially on systems that support business operations.

The company also says customer test data stays within the ThreatBook environment and is not sent to third-party agents. RedAgents supports Zero Data Retention, or ZDR, which ThreatBook says enables complete deletion of test data.

Security teams should confirm how these controls work in practice, including retention periods, access permissions, logging and any contractual terms, before submitting sensitive environment details.

The launch comes as more security products use AI agents to automate parts of testing. Other examples covered by Cybersecurity News include PentestCode’s AI testing agent and Xalgorix’s verification-focused platform.

These products differ in how they are deployed and how they handle findings, so teams should compare scope controls, evidence quality and data handling rather than treating “AI pentesting” as one uniform category.

The main promise of RedAgents is breadth: multiple agents may explore a target in different ways and give teams a combined view of possible weaknesses.

That does not guarantee that every result is valid or that every vulnerability will be found. Security staff still need to review evidence, reproduce important findings safely and prioritize fixes based on business impact and exposure.

ThreatBook says the platform can reduce false positives by combining agent results, but the announcement does not publish independent accuracy figures or a false-positive rate.

It also does not identify a specific customer deployment, measured security outcome or external validation of the service. Those details will matter to organizations assessing whether the platform fits their testing process.

RedAgents’ stated distinction is not a single testing method but a central platform for selecting and coordinating several agents. ThreatBook says it plans to add more open-source agents over time, alongside the enterprise tools available at launch.

Businesses and individuals are not prohibited from using DeepSeek by this order. U.S. Government Bans DeepSeek AI The DHS notice sets out two requirements. Federal civilian agencies must exclude DeepSeek and affiliate IT products and services from procurement. They must also remove DeepSeek and affiliate products, including covered third-party implementations, from agency technology systems. That second requirement makes the order broader than a block on new purchases. The third-party provision is especially important for security teams. An agency may use DeepSeek through another supplier rather than through an application carrying the DeepSeek name. A review limited to branded chat tools could therefore miss products covered by the removal requirement. Agencies need to establish what powers their existing AI services. The notice does not provide a public list of every affected third-party vendor or product. Suppliers and agency buyers will need to assess whether particular tools use DeepSeek implementations, rather than assuming that a different product name places them outside the order. Contract records and technical documentation can help support that review. For vendors serving civilian agencies, the order also raises a direct procurement question. For agencies, the question is no longer only whether a chatbot gives accurate answers or whether staff should upload sensitive files. They must also know which companies and underlying technologies support the software they buy, deploy, and connect to government systems. items.title: Meta glasses caught recording conversations without wake phrase
items.summary: Meta says it has resolved an issue after some Ray-Ban Meta owners reported that their glasses recorded conversations without the “Hey Meta” wake phrase. Users reported finding recordings and transcripts of conversations they did not knowingly save. Recording without anyone realizing raises privacy concerns for both the wearer and the people around them. The complaints surfaced on Reddit , where one owner described unexpected recordings occurring with three pairs of glasses. The owner said the behavior started after a firmware update and occurred even with Respond without Hey Meta disabled. They also reported that the glasses’ internal notification light sometimes activated during normal conversation. Other commenters described similar unexplained activations. As Android Authority reports , Meta says the problem has been fixed: “This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.” What’s missing is a public explanation of what caused it, how many people were affected, and what happened to the audio captured. This isn’t the first time we’ve reported on privacy concerns involving smart glasses. In June, we covered unreleased facial-recognition code found in Meta’s companion app . The code was not active, but the reporting raised concerns about how wearable cameras could eventually move from capturing people to identifying them without their knowledge. What owners can do According to the Reddit owner, Meta Support recommended disabling microphone and camera permissions, turning off Wear Detection , deleting voice history, and disabling automatic updates. Those steps would limit much of the gadget’s core functionality without explaining what went wrong. Until Meta provides a fuller explanation, here are a few precautions that make sense if you wish to keep using your smart glasses: Review your voice history. Look for interactions you do not recognize and delete unwanted recordings or transcripts. Meta says users can manage these logs through Settings . Check your voice-activation settings. The owner reporting the issue said Respond without Hey Meta was already disabled, so do not treat that setting alone as a guarantee against unintended activation. Keep the glasses and companion app updated. Although the user associated the behavior with an update, that is not a good reason to permanently abandon updates that may contain security and privacy fixes. Always ask before recording other people. Their privacy matters even when your glasses are working exactly as intended. Meta still owes users an explanation of what went wrong and what it has done to ensure it won’t happen again. Browse like no one’s watching. items.title: Hackers Exploit Palo Alto VPN Flaw to Bypass MFA and Steal Credentials From VMware Disks
items.summary: Ransomware operators are exploiting a Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect VPN flaw to bypass multi-factor authentication and enter corporate networks. In one investigated case, attackers reached VMware management systems and stole credentials directly from a domain controller’s virtual disk, avoiding security tools running inside the virtual machine. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed the activity in an October 19 threat brief update . Researchers linked exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 to Spikey Scorpius, also known as Qilin, and Tarnished Scorpius, also known as Inc. Separate public reporting connected exploitation to operators using Settra ransomware. Investigations ongoing since early June have covered healthcare, education, financial services, manufacturing, government, energy, and other sectors. The latest findings show how unauthorized VPN access can develop into credential theft, data theft, and ransomware deployment. GlobalProtect Flaw Bypasses MFA The vulnerability affects GlobalProtect portals and gateways in certain PAN-OS and Prisma Access deployments. Exposure requires authentication override cookies to be enabled alongside a vulnerable certificate setup. Palo Alto Networks rates the flaw High, with a CVSS score of 7.8 and its highest suggested response urgency. Panorama and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Authentication override cookies let previously authenticated users reconnect without repeating the full login process. According to Rapid7’s technical analysis , vulnerable devices decrypt these cookies but do not properly verify that a trusted system created them. If the cookie certificate is reused for a publicly exposed service, attackers can obtain its public key and forge a cookie. The gateway may accept that cookie as proof of authentication, allowing a VPN connection without the normal login and MFA checks. Cybersecurity News previously covered this GlobalProtect authentication bypass . After establishing access, attackers use remote monitoring and management tools to explore internal networks. They move between systems through Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block, then prepare tools for credential harvesting, data theft, and ransomware deployment. The most notable case involved a move from the compromised VPN gateway to VMware’s vCenter management appliance. Attackers then disabled the execInstalledOnly security control on ESXi hosts and used a custom tool to extract credentials offline from a domain controller’s VMDK virtual disk. Unit 42 did not name the tool or provide its implementation details. Reading credentials directly from the disk bypasses endpoint detection and response controls inside the affected virtual machine. The approach targets the infrastructure beneath the operating system rather than relying on a credential-stealing program running within it. Cybersecurity News has also reported on VMware attacks involving detached domain controller disks . Unit 42 also observed attackers combining this initial access with tools targeting Veeam backup infrastructure through CVE-2023-27532. That separate flaw can expose encrypted credentials stored in the backup configuration database, potentially opening access to backup hosts. Defenders should examine GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events linked to suspicious sources and client details. Reported indicators include 104.207.144[.]154 , 146.19.216[.]125 , device names GP-CLIENT and DESKTOP-GP01 , and host IDs aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55 . Earlier monitoring found that many probes did not establish full VPN sessions, making connection events important for investigation. Organizations should follow the Palo Alto Networks advisory and upgrade every affected portal and gateway.
