Man seeking love travels 2,000 km to meet an AI-generated woman
items.summary: A 49-year-old bricklayer sold his belongings before traveling 2,000 km by bus from his home in Brazil to meet “Jéssica,” an online influencer he had fallen for. Yet despite having a social media account with more than 300,000 followers, she never existed. Edimar Rocha Martins lives in Imperatriz, a city in northeastern Brazil. He says he struck up an online conversation with Jéssica Fazendeira, who supposedly lived near the southeastern city of Belo Horizonte. The AI persona promising love The online persona’s name, “Fazendeira,” loosely translates as “female farmer.” She described herself as living on a farm. Martins said that he had been talking with the persona online since 2020. He decided to visit her after she offered to pay for his trip and have him live on the farm with her, he said. The account’s operator disputes this, saying the character was created in 2025 and denying any private messages with him. A video posted on one of her online accounts (captured here by Brazilian news service Imirante) asked for a man to come and live with her and offered to fund the trip. The AI-generated farmer says, translated: I’m not joking, my intentions are serious. I want to meet someone who wants to build something real and beautiful with me. If you’re a simple man who likes peace and quiet and a calm life, then maybe we’d get along really well. After selling his possessions to fund the bus trip, Martins arrived in Belo Horizonte and began asking about the woman. Unable to find her, he approached a local radio station, where staff explained that she was an AI-generated character. Without enough money to return, he received food, support, and a bus ticket to Augustinópolis, in Tocantins, from the city’s migrant assistance service. He later returned to Imperatriz, where he stayed with relatives. The account’s operator hits back The account’s administrator posted a message through the AI character’s TikTok account denying any kind of scam. Translated, it said: This profile is pretty much abandoned, but I’ve come here to state the obvious. I’m made of artificial intelligence , and I’ve never talked to anyone on this profile. The aim was to get engagement for sales. I never spoke directly to anyone, much less brought anyone to Belo Horizonte. The operator told reporters that the character was created to attract viewers and promote products through affiliate sales. They said they did not know whether other people had reused the character’s content on other accounts. Another video shows messages people have reportedly sent the account, with the character explaining that it keeps telling viewers it’s an AI. It complains: And then it’s still my fault, right? These people are lost. In another video, where it is being interviewed by an AI-generated male character, the persona explains that it deactivated and then reactivated its account. It said: I was the first AI to get canceled for absolutely nothing. These are scripted responses published through a fictional character, rather than an AI independently defending itself. Police said they could not establish at that stage whether a crime had occurred. One outlet reported that Martins has been struggling with loneliness following his mother’s death. Videos published to the reactivated TikTok account are labeled as AI generated. It also links to an Instagram account with videos of the character, where videos carry similar labels. Those current labels don’t establish what Martins saw before his trip. Social media already encourages parasocial relationships, where viewers feel a personal connection with someone who doesn’t know them. AI-generated personas add another complication: The person viewers feel connected to may be entirely fictional. In our Face value report , 88% of adults surveyed said it’s becoming harder to tell what online content is genuinely human or real. The AI plot thickens June saw reports of a 72-year-old man who traveled 4,000 km from his home in Boa Vista to … Belo Horizonte. He visited after seeing a farm woman on a social network who was offering a job opportunity and perhaps something more. Unable to return home, he sought help from social workers. In August, 71-year-old Alberto da Costa traveled from Manaus to the same city after watching videos featuring the same woman, according to Itatiaia. He paid almost R$3,000 for a flight, then sought help from the outlet when he couldn’t afford to return home. The videos simulated personal conversations, giving viewers the impression that the woman was speaking directly to them. The account reportedly had nearly a million followers. The reporting doesn’t establish whether this woman was AI-generated or whether the account was connected to Jéssica’s. Nor does it establish that the men sent money to the account operators. But the costs can still be real: selling possessions, paying for travel, and finding yourself stranded far from home. Protect yourself and others The same advice applies here as to romance scams, but with some extras. Don’t send money or travel to see someone you’ve never met without independently checking who they are. Don’t rely on video calls alone. Scammers now use deepfake video calls to dupe victims live. And check whether you’re exchanging private messages or watching public videos that anyone can see. Look for information beyond the account itself. Search their name and profile pictures, and research where they say they work. Be cautious if their story doesn’t add up or they avoid questions about their identity. When you feel close to someone, questioning that connection can be difficult. Before sending money or booking travel, talk to a friend or family member and get their perspective. And if you’re worried about someone who may be in a similar situation, check in without judgment and offer to look through the account together. Images courtesy of Jam Press Something feel off? And then it’s still my fault, right? These people are lost.

In another video, where it is being interviewed by an AI-generated male character, the persona explains that it deactivated and then reactivated its account. It said:

I was the first AI to get canceled for absolutely nothing.

These are scripted responses published through a fictional character, rather than an AI independently defending itself.

Police said they could not establish at that stage whether a crime had occurred.

One outlet reported that Martins has been struggling with loneliness following his mother’s death.

Videos published to the reactivated TikTok account are labeled as AI generated. It also links to an Instagram account with videos of the character, where videos carry similar labels. Those current labels don’t establish what Martins saw before his trip.

Social media already encourages parasocial relationships, where viewers feel a personal connection with someone who doesn’t know them. AI-generated personas add another complication: The person viewers feel connected to may be entirely fictional.

In our Face value report, 88% of adults surveyed said it’s becoming harder to tell what online content is genuinely human or real.

The AI plot thickens

June saw reports of a 72-year-old man who traveled 4,000 km from his home in Boa Vista to … Belo Horizonte. He visited after seeing a farm woman on a social network who was offering a job opportunity and perhaps something more. Unable to return home, he sought help from social workers.

In August, 71-year-old Alberto da Costa traveled from Manaus to the same city after watching videos featuring the same woman, according to Itatiaia. He paid almost R$3,000 for a flight, then sought help from the outlet when he couldn’t afford to return home.

The videos simulated personal conversations, giving viewers the impression that the woman was speaking directly to them. The account reportedly had nearly a million followers.

The reporting doesn’t establish whether this woman was AI-generated or whether the account was connected to Jéssica’s. Nor does it establish that the men sent money to the account operators. But the costs can still be real: selling possessions, paying for travel, and finding yourself stranded far from home.

Protect yourself and others

The same advice applies here as to romance scams, but with some extras. Don’t send money or travel to see someone you’ve never met without independently checking who they are.

Don’t rely on video calls alone. Scammers now use deepfake video calls to dupe victims live. And check whether you’re exchanging private messages or watching public videos that anyone can see.

Look for information beyond the account itself. Search their name and profile pictures, and research where they say they work. Be cautious if their story doesn’t add up or they avoid questions about their identity.

When you feel close to someone, questioning that connection can be difficult. Before sending money or booking travel, talk to a friend or family member and get their perspective. And if you’re worried about someone who may be in a similar situation, check in without judgment and offer to look through the account together.

items.summary: For many organizations, GitHub Enterprise serves as a central platform for software development, collaboration, and source code management. This makes it an increasingly valuable target for attackers seeking access to source code, sensitive information, credentials, and development infrastructure. Recent incidents demonstrate an increasing preference among attackers for targeting GitHub environments. In March 2026, the Trivy supply-chain attack involved stolen credentials being used to publish malicious releases and tamper with GitHub Actions. The compromise subsequently extended to Checkmarx’s GitHub environment, where attackers gained unauthorized repository access and distributed malicious code through developer tools and CI/CD . In May 2026, GitHub itself disclosed that an employee device had been compromised through a malicious VS Code extension, resulting in the exfiltration of internal repositories . In May 2026, a reported exposure of sensitive CISA information through a public GitHub repository highlighted how misconfigured access and unintended data disclosure can expose sensitive information. These incidents highlight the growing importance of protecting and monitoring code repositories. Sign in to GitHub with an enterprise owner account and navigate to Settings . Open Audit log and select L og streaming . Create a new audit log stream and configure the destination where the logs will be sent. 4. items.summary_html:
For many organizations, GitHub Enterprise serves as a central platform for software development, collaboration, and source code management. This makes it an increasingly valuable target for attackers seeking access to source code, sensitive information, credentials, and development infrastructure.

Recent incidents demonstrate an increasing preference among attackers for targeting GitHub environments. In March 2026, the Trivy supply-chain attack involved stolen credentials being used to publish malicious releases and tamper with GitHub Actions. The compromise subsequently extended to Checkmarx’s GitHub environment, where attackers gained unauthorized repository access and distributed malicious code through developer tools and CI/CD. In May 2026, GitHub itself disclosed that an employee device had been compromised through a malicious VS Code extension, resulting in the exfiltration of internal repositories. In May 2026, a reported exposure of sensitive CISA information through a public GitHub repository highlighted how misconfigured access and unintended data disclosure can expose sensitive information. These incidents highlight the growing importance of protecting and monitoring code repositories.

Tools such as GitHound, a BloodHound OpenGraph collector for GitHub released by SpecterOps earlier in 2026, can help defenders map a GitHub organization’s environment by identifying relationships between users, teams, repositories, and permissions that allows them to understand access relationships, identify excessive privileges, and uncover potential attack paths. However, the same capabilities can also be leveraged by adversaries to map an organization’s GitHub environment, discover accessible resources, and identify opportunities for further access.

With this in mind, I took a closer look at GitHub Enterprise audit logs and weather they can be used to detect enumeration through the GitHub API.

Running GitHound Against a GitHub Organization

GitHound interacts directly with the GitHub API to collect information about an organization’s users, teams, repositories, and permissions. To do so, it requires a GitHub access token with the appropriate permissions to access the resources being queried. The scope of the collected data therefore depends on the token’s privileges.

Step 1: Create a GitHub personal access token

To authenticate GitHound, create a personal access token (PAT) on GitHub.

  1. Navigate to GitHub’s personal access token settings for your account.
  2. Select Tokens, then click Generate new token.
  3. Provide a descriptive name and set an appropriate expiration date.
  4. Configure the repository access and permissions required for the resources you intend to collect. Use the GitHub documentation to understand the available permissions.
  5. Generate the token and copy it immediately.
Step 2: Run GitHound against the Organization

The next step would be to download and run GitHound. Download the tool from the official SpecterOps repo.

To run GitHound against your organization open a powershell session and run the following commands:

  1. Load the collector:
. ./githound.ps1
GitHound module loading

2. Create a session with your Personal Access Token

$session = New-GitHubSession -OrganizationName "" -Token ""
GitHound session variable creation

3. Run the collection script

Invoke-GitHound -Session $session

or 

Invoke-GitHound -Session $session -CollectAll
GitHound executionGitHub Logging Configuration

As GitHound makes API requests to enumerate these resources, its activity will be visible in GitHub audit logs, providing an opportunity for defenders to investigate and detect potentially suspicious patterns of API usage. Before building a detection for GitHub API enumeration though, it is important to ensure that the relevant audit events are being collected.

  1. Sign in to GitHub with an enterprise owner account and navigate to Settings.
  2. Open Audit log and select Log streaming. For our tests we are selecting streaming to Azure Blob Storage to ingest the logs to Microsoft Sentinel via the GitHub data connector from Microsoft’s Content Hub.
  3. Create a new audit log stream and configure the destination where the logs will be sent.

4. In the Settings tab, enable the option to Enable API Request Events so that API activity is captured alongside other audit events.

5. Save the configuration and verify that events are arriving at the configured destination.

For detailed instructions refer to GitHub’s official documentation: Streaming the audit log for your enterprise.

Building the Detection

Sure enough, GitHound’s API activity is visible in the GitHub audit logs, providing an opportunity to detect the enumeration through Microsoft Sentinel.

GitHound enumeration activity

The query focuses on API routes commonly used to retrieve organizational information, including repositories, teams, permissions, and GitHub Actions configuration. It counts the distinct routes and URL paths accessed by an actor and compares these counts against predefined thresholds to identify potential enumeration activity. While this behavior is consistent with GitHound, the detection identifies an enumeration pattern rather than this specific tool.

let route_threshold = 10;
let url_path_threshold = 20;
let routes_of_intrest = dynamic([@'/graphql', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles/:role_id/teams', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/secrets', @'/organizations/:organization_id/custom-repository-roles', @'/organizations/:organization_id/repos', @'/organizations/:organization_id/secret-scanning/alerts', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles/:role_id/users', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions/self-hosted-runners', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/variables', @'/organizations/:organization_id', @'/organizations/:organization_id/actions/permissions/workflow', @'/organizations/:organization_id/organization-roles', @'/organizations/:organization_id/teams']);
GitHubAuditLogsV3_CL
| where Action == "api.request"
| project-reorder UrlPath, Route, RequestMethod, QueryString, StatusCode, UserAgent
| where Route in~ (routes_of_intrest)
| summarize
    c = count(),
    RequestMethod = make_set(RequestMethod),
    StatusCode = make_set(StatusCode),
    Route = make_set(Route),
    UrlPath = make_set(UrlPath),
    UserAgent = make_set(UserAgent),
    User = make_set(User),
    OperationType = make_set(OperationType),
    Org = make_set(Org),
    OrgId = make_set(OrgId),
    ActorId = make_set(ActorId),
    ActorIsBot = make_set(ActorIsBot),
    ProgrammaticAccessType = make_set(ProgrammaticAccessType),
    TokenScopes = make_set(TokenScopes),
    Type = make_set(Type),
    Action = make_set(Action),
    Business = make_set(Business)
by Actor, TokenId
| extend RouteCount = array_length(Route)
| extend UrlPathCount = array_length(UrlPath)
| where RouteCount > route_threshold or UrlPathCount > url_path_threshold
GitHub API enumeration query resultsClosing Thoughts

GitHub API enumeration can provide attackers with valuable insight into an organization’s repositories, permissions, and development workflows, making API monitoring essential for protecting development environments.

In this blog post, we demonstrated how GitHound’s activity can be observed in GitHub audit logs and how we can detect the API enumeration pattern. By enabling API request logging and implementing this or similar detections, defenders can improve visibility across their GitHub Enterprise environment and identify suspicious activity at an early stage.

Detecting GitHound Enumeration via the GitHub API was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware
items.summary: Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases. The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the cloud provider, which blocked the malicious files within 94 minutes. OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba said the affected releases were v0.11.0, v0.12.0, v0.13.0, v0.14.0, and v0.15.0. He identified v0.10.0 as clean and announced a safe v0.16.0 release. That replacement is now available on the project’s official GitHub releases page , where it is marked as immutable, meaning its published release files cannot be changed. OVHcloud Supply Chain Attack According to Klaba’s account, the compromised files appeared at 14:47 and were detected and blocked at 16:21. OVHcloud’s initial checks found no other affected repository. Those findings limit the confirmed scope to the CLI project, rather than establishing a wider breach across the company’s GitHub organization or cloud platform. The attacker used an existing developer account to add a malicious binary to the software distributed through GitHub. This placed the threat inside a trusted download location, giving users little reason to suspect that a routine CLI download could expose local credentials. OVHcloud has not explained how the developer account was first compromised. The customer’s report raised concerns about release files being replaced with a “dirty build” of a later commit. In software builds, that label generally signals changes beyond the recorded source revision. The public issue listing identifies the report as issue #300, covering replaced assets for v0.13.0 through v0.15.0. OVHcloud’s warning named two additional affected versions. The customer also questioned the account behind the changes and asked whether release files should be locked against replacement. They said they had switched to building through the Go module proxy while seeking clarification. Their report was public because the repository lacked a private vulnerability reporting channel. Klaba described the added program as a binary whose job was to retrieve secrets from disk. He said its quality was poor but warned that it could still achieve its purpose. The available disclosure does not establish which files it searched, where collected data was sent, or how many users executed the malicious downloads. The CLI’s normal role makes this threat especially serious. OVHcloud documents the tool as a way to manage cloud services, account resources, and automated workflows. Its supported authentication methods include a local .ovh.conf file containing credentials, alongside environment variables for application keys, application secrets, and consumer keys. Those documented credential locations explain why a compromised administration tool can create risks beyond the downloaded program itself. However, they are not a confirmed list of this malware’s targets. Until OVHcloud publishes its technical findings, specific claims about stolen SSH keys, browser passwords, persistence, or attacker infrastructure would go beyond the evidence. The incident fits the broader pattern covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s reporting on trusted software updates used to steal developer and cloud credentials . Attackers can use stolen publishing access to turn familiar software delivery channels into routes for credential theft, without needing users to visit a fake website. OVHcloud urged users who downloaded the CLI during the incident to update it immediately or delete it. Klaba also advised affected users to change all secrets stored on disk. Rotation is important because replacing the malicious program does not cancel credentials that may already have been copied. Organizations investigating possible exposure should identify which machines downloaded and ran affected files, preserve available evidence, and review account activity tied to potentially exposed credentials. Their response should extend beyond OVHcloud credentials if other secrets were accessible on those machines. The company’s warning covers local secrets broadly, not only its own service keys. A related GhostAction GitHub credential theft campaign shows why repository access deserves close attention. That campaign used stolen accounts to introduce malicious workflows under trusted identities. No evidence currently links it to the OVHcloud incident. For OVHcloud users, the immediate priorities remain replacing affected downloads and renewing potentially exposed secrets while the company continues its malware investigation and publishes further technical findings.

items.title: Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates for Just 5 Minutes to Secretly Install Backdoors
items.summary: A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant found that attackers repeatedly altered AOMEI’s update settings for only a few minutes at a time between April and July 2026. Any AOMEI Backupper computer checking for updates during an active window could receive a malicious download instead of a genuine update. The operation did not rely on a software flaw or require users to open a suspicious file. Instead, the attackers changed two configuration files on AOMEI’s servers, redirecting downloads and using the program’s notification feature to run the malware. Affected organizations were reported across several sectors and countries, including India, though the full number of impacted systems is not known. Google Cloud’s GTIG and Mandiant analysts tracked the malware chain as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD and attributed the activity to a threat group they call UNC7017. The initial activity was first detected through telemetry shared by ManageEngine’s Threat Analysis Lab, which observed suspicious behavior in late May. AOMEI told Google that it had taken corrective action to secure its distribution servers. Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates AOMEI’s update process uses down_html.ini to provide a package version, checksum and download location. A separate file, Notifycfg.ini , guides its notification service, including which local programs to run. During observed tampering periods, attackers changed both files so the software would accept and launch a harmful ZIP archive. Researchers recorded three specific windows: ten minutes on May 28, six minutes on July 16 and five minutes on July 20. The attackers restored the original settings after each window. AOMEI Update Mechanism (Source – Google Cloud) That made ordinary checks of the live update server less useful: an investigation carried out later could see only the clean files. The method differs from incidents involving altered software releases or build systems; a Notepad++ update breach is another example of attackers targeting the route that delivers trusted software. The brief windows did not make the malware itself temporary. A computer that received the altered instructions could continue running malicious files after AOMEI’s servers were repaired. In July, the attackers also directed one download through a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, after earlier use of Alibaba Cloud storage and domains designed to look connected to AOMEI. This changing delivery setup could make simple domain-blocking rules less reliable. How the malware chain worked The first-stage program, CROSSROAD, arrived as upgrade-now.exe . It checked aspects of the computer and could download additional files, create a scheduled task and then delete its own copy. The task launched a legitimate Radmin program every three hours. However, the Radmin process was placed alongside an attacker-created DLL named BlkScrDl.dll , which it loaded during startup. That DLL helped start SHINYROAD, a backdoor that could communicate with the attackers’ systems. Later activity also involved ADAPTAGENT, a client for the Adaptix command-and-control framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software. Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic (Source – Google Cloud) The use of real administration software and familiar product names can make a malicious process harder to distinguish from normal activity. Other recent incidents, such as the DAEMON Tools malware supply-chain case , show how attackers can abuse trusted software channels to reach users. On July 20, attackers added a second risk. They used an invisible, one-pixel notification window to make an AOMEI client request a remote file over WebDAV. That request could prompt Windows to send NetNTLMv2 authentication data to an attacker-controlled server without a visible prompt. This technique is known as credential coercion: the victim’s computer is induced to attempt authentication to a remote location. AOMEI’s server-side fix does not remove files already installed on affected computers. Organizations using AOMEI software should review endpoint and network records covering the campaign period, paying particular attention to unusual updater child processes, unexpected Radmin or Nitro-related scheduled tasks, and connections to the indicators below. Analysts should also examine cached AOMEI configuration files and relevant proxy or firewall logs, since the live server may now return legitimate settings. The incident also highlights a design issue for software vendors: HTTPS and a checksum supplied in an unsigned configuration file are not enough to prove an update is genuine. Google recommends signed configuration files, cryptographic verification of downloaded files, and strict limits on which domains an updater may contact. Separating promotional pop-ups from update execution can also reduce the risk of one feature being misused to launch code. The case echoes other short-lived supply-chain incidents, including a LiteLLM package compromise in which malicious releases were available for a limited period. In both situations, a brief exposure window can still leave behind a longer incident-response task: find affected systems, assess what ran, and investigate whether credentials or other access were exposed. A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant found that attackers repeatedly altered AOMEI’s update settings for only a few minutes at a time between April and July 2026.

Any AOMEI Backupper computer checking for updates during an active window could receive a malicious download instead of a genuine update.

The operation did not rely on a software flaw or require users to open a suspicious file. Instead, the attackers changed two configuration files on AOMEI’s servers, redirecting downloads and using the program’s notification feature to run the malware.

Affected organizations were reported across several sectors and countries, including India, though the full number of impacted systems is not known.

Google Cloud’s GTIG and Mandiant analysts tracked the malware chain as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD and attributed the activity to a threat group they call UNC7017.

The initial activity was first detected through telemetry shared by ManageEngine’s Threat Analysis Lab, which observed suspicious behavior in late May. AOMEI told Google that it had taken corrective action to secure its distribution servers.

Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates

AOMEI’s update process uses down_html.ini to provide a package version, checksum and download location. A separate file, Notifycfg.ini, guides its notification service, including which local programs to run.

During observed tampering periods, attackers changed both files so the software would accept and launch a harmful ZIP archive.

Researchers recorded three specific windows: ten minutes on May 28, six minutes on July 16 and five minutes on July 20. The attackers restored the original settings after each window.

AOMEI Update Mechanism (Source – Google Cloud)

That made ordinary checks of the live update server less useful: an investigation carried out later could see only the clean files.

The method differs from incidents involving altered software releases or build systems; a Notepad++ update breach is another example of attackers targeting the route that delivers trusted software.

The brief windows did not make the malware itself temporary. A computer that received the altered instructions could continue running malicious files after AOMEI’s servers were repaired.

In July, the attackers also directed one download through a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, after earlier use of Alibaba Cloud storage and domains designed to look connected to AOMEI. This changing delivery setup could make simple domain-blocking rules less reliable.

How the malware chain worked

The first-stage program, CROSSROAD, arrived as upgrade-now.exe. It checked aspects of the computer and could download additional files, create a scheduled task and then delete its own copy.

The task launched a legitimate Radmin program every three hours. However, the Radmin process was placed alongside an attacker-created DLL named BlkScrDl.dll, which it loaded during startup.

That DLL helped start SHINYROAD, a backdoor that could communicate with the attackers’ systems. Later activity also involved ADAPTAGENT, a client for the Adaptix command-and-control framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software.

Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic (Source – Google Cloud)

The use of real administration software and familiar product names can make a malicious process harder to distinguish from normal activity.

Other recent incidents, such as the DAEMON Tools malware supply-chain case, show how attackers can abuse trusted software channels to reach users.

On July 20, attackers added a second risk. They used an invisible, one-pixel notification window to make an AOMEI client request a remote file over WebDAV.

That request could prompt Windows to send NetNTLMv2 authentication data to an attacker-controlled server without a visible prompt. This technique is known as credential coercion: the victim’s computer is induced to attempt authentication to a remote location.

AOMEI’s server-side fix does not remove files already installed on affected computers. Organizations using AOMEI software should review endpoint and network records covering the campaign period, paying particular attention to unusual updater child processes, unexpected Radmin or Nitro-related scheduled tasks, and connections to the indicators below.

Analysts should also examine cached AOMEI configuration files and relevant proxy or firewall logs, since the live server may now return legitimate settings.

The incident also highlights a design issue for software vendors: HTTPS and a checksum supplied in an unsigned configuration file are not enough to prove an update is genuine.

Google recommends signed configuration files, cryptographic verification of downloaded files, and strict limits on which domains an updater may contact. Separating promotional pop-ups from update execution can also reduce the risk of one feature being misused to launch code.

The case echoes other short-lived supply-chain incidents, including a LiteLLM package compromise in which malicious releases were available for a limited period.

In both situations, a brief exposure window can still leave behind a longer incident-response task: find affected systems, assess what ran, and investigate whether credentials or other access were exposed.

items.title: Hackers Compromise Rank Math PRO WordPress Plugin to Install Self-Rebuilding Backdoors
items.summary: Hackers planted malware in copies of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin, exposing websites to hidden backdoors that can rebuild themselves after removal. Rank Math confirmed that some version 3.0.123 packages distributed during a limited October download window contained malicious code that could compromise websites when activated. The company removed the affected files and released clean version 3.0.124. The affected window ran from October 15, 2026, at 20:02 UTC to October 16 at 07:12 UTC. Rank Math described the impact as limited but did not provide an affected website count in its security advisory. The free Rank Math SEO plugin available through WordPress.org is not affected, and its users need no action for this incident. Website owners who installed and activated an affected package must treat their sites as compromised. Installing the clean release alone does not complete recovery because malicious files, database entries, accounts, or server changes may remain. Users who installed the package without activating it should delete it, install the clean version, and run a precautionary scan. Downloading it without installation or activation does not establish compromise. Rank Math PRO Backdoor Survives Removal Rank Math warns that the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits an infected website. Deleting a suspicious PHP file may therefore provide only temporary relief while the components responsible for restoring it remain active. Deactivating the plugin is also insufficient, according to the vendor’s recovery guidance. Manual cleanup must begin by deleting the entire rank-math-pro directory. Administrators must then remove malicious records from the WordPress options table before hunting for remaining backdoors. Rank Math lists three suspicious option_name values, _uf6qdn2hmm , t8krdk990phb , and _np5pvf754c . Where supported, hosting providers or firewalls should also block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com . The vendor identifies several places where hidden PHP files may appear, including wp-content/mu-plugins/ , other plugin folders, non-default theme directories, and Rank Math’s includes/ folder. Investigators should look for base64_decode combined with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn , proc_open , or PHP-FPM socket code. These are investigation clues that require review within the surrounding file. Additional warning signs include unfamiliar administrator accounts with usernames beginning wpsupport_ or email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net . Rank Math also identifies wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php as a fake core file. Its guidance calls for checking .htaccess rules that allow .cache files to execute as PHP and system cron entries tagged #ms6v46 . These checks cover several possible routes back into a cleaned website. The cleanup challenge resembles earlier self-healing WordPress malware covered by Cyber Security News, where surviving components restored deleted files. Separately, a BdThemes supply chain attack showed how trusted plugin features could become a path to account takeover and persistent access. Neither comparison establishes a link between those attackers and this incident. Recovery Requires More Than a Plugin Update. Rank Math recommends restoring both website files and the database from a clean backup made before October 15 at 20:02 UTC. Restoring only plugin files could leave malicious database content untouched. After restoration, owners should scan the site, replace exposed credentials, and install Rank Math PRO 3.0.124 from their account. Without a suitable backup, owners need a wider investigation after disabling the rebuilding mechanism. That includes checking users, scheduled WordPress events, uploads, plugins, and themes. The vendor also recommends reviewing SSH authorized_keys , running processes, other users’ crontabs, and writable locations outside the website directory. Shared hosting customers should ask their provider to examine areas they cannot access. All secrets accessible to the compromised website should be treated as potentially exposed, even after a backup restore. Rank Math advises replacing WordPress passwords, database credentials, security keys and salts, payment gateway keys, SMTP credentials, API keys, and hosting access credentials. Administrator two-factor authentication settings also require review. This is precautionary guidance, not confirmation that every affected site suffered data theft. Finally, owners should scan with tools such as Wordfence or Sucuri and run wp core verify-checksums . Premium plugins may lack public checksums, requiring comparison with official clean copies. Monitor outgoing connections and returning files over subsequent days. Rank Math urges users to visit its website directly and warns that it will not email login or download links. items.title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
items.summary: Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure. Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements. These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve. Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate. Sovereign Control Panel , entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required. This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian , which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger , also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed. Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure. Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms , now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information. Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements. Designing for resilience and operational independence For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption. To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns . These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed. For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions. For workloads that require greater operational independence, Sovereign Private Cloud extends that continuum into customer-operated environments. It supports connected and disconnected operating models. The ability to transition workloads from connected to disconnected operations is entering public preview, giving organizations greater flexibility to sustain critical services as connectivity and operating requirements change. Bringing more of the application lifecycle under local control Operational independence requires more than infrastructure. Increasingly, organizations need data, development tools, model capabilities and productivity services their applications depend on to operate within the same customer-controlled environment. Sovereign Private Cloud, built on Azure Local, extends Microsoft cloud capabilities into environments that customers operate and control. SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments. DocumentDB and Blob Storage on Azure Local are both entering public preview, giving organizations more choice in how they run and manage critical data within customer-controlled environments. GitHub Enterprise Local will become generally available at Microsoft Ignite as a validated GitHub Enterprise Server appliance on Azure Local, helping organizations keep repositories, code and development artifacts under local control. Developers can also use GitHub Copilot with locally hosted models for inference, bringing AI-assisted development closer to their code and data within the environments they control. The local application environment is expanding with Foundry Local . At Ignite, Foundry Local will become generally available for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local, with an expanded model catalog that includes Microsoft, partner, open-weight and open-source models. Local inference and agentic retrieval will also enable users to interact with local enterprise data using natural language and receive responses grounded in that data. Integration with Microsoft 365 Local , available in preview for approved customers, extends this functionality to locally operated Microsoft SharePoint and Exchange servers. Confidential virtual machines on Azure Local are generally available, extending confidential computing capabilities to customer-controlled infrastructure. Hardware-encrypted memory and hardware-based isolation help protect sensitive data while it is being processed. Workload attestation adds assurance before sensitive data or keys are released. For regulated, sensitive and mission-critical workloads, these safeguards provide another layer of protection while giving organizations greater control over where their data and applications run. Azure Local will support multitenancy , allowing organizations to separate resources, governance and management across multiple tenants while sharing the underlying infrastructure. This significantly expands what customers with distinct business units or security boundaries can achieve with Sovereign Private Cloud. Multitenancy also creates new opportunities for local operators and service providers to deliver differentiated sovereign cloud services on Azure Local infrastructure. These additions bring more of the application lifecycle under local control, spanning data, development, productivity, AI and operations. Organizations can determine what runs locally based on the requirements of each workload. Extending the continuum through partners Navigating sovereignty is increasingly complex. Regulatory, security, operational and business requirements vary across countries, industries and workloads. Organizations must translate these needs into technology and operating models that work in their local context. items.summary_html:
Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require.

This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate.

Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work.

A continuum of control, built around the workload

Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model.

Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure.

Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements.

These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve.

Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud

For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate.

Sovereign Control Panel, entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required.

This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian, which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger, also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed.

Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure.

Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms, now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information.

Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements.

Designing for resilience and operational independence

For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption.

To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns. These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed.

For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions. For workloads that require greater operational independence, Sovereign Private Cloud extends that continuum into customer-operated environments. It supports connected and disconnected operating models. The ability to transition workloads from connected to disconnected operations is entering public preview, giving organizations greater flexibility to sustain critical services as connectivity and operating requirements change.

Bringing more of the application lifecycle under local control

Operational independence requires more than infrastructure. Increasingly, organizations need data, development tools, model capabilities and productivity services their applications depend on to operate within the same customer-controlled environment.

Sovereign Private Cloud, built on Azure Local, extends Microsoft cloud capabilities into environments that customers operate and control. SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments. DocumentDB and Blob Storage on Azure Local are both entering public preview, giving organizations more choice in how they run and manage critical data within customer-controlled environments.

GitHub Enterprise Local will become generally available at Microsoft Ignite as a validated GitHub Enterprise Server appliance on Azure Local, helping organizations keep repositories, code and development artifacts under local control. Developers can also use GitHub Copilot with locally hosted models for inference, bringing AI-assisted development closer to their code and data within the environments they control.

The local application environment is expanding with Foundry Local. At Ignite, Foundry Local will become generally available for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local, with an expanded model catalog that includes Microsoft, partner, open-weight and open-source models. Local inference and agentic retrieval will also enable users to interact with local enterprise data using natural language and receive responses grounded in that data. Integration with Microsoft 365 Local, available in preview for approved customers, extends this functionality to locally operated Microsoft SharePoint and Exchange servers.

Confidential virtual machines on Azure Local are generally available, extending confidential computing capabilities to customer-controlled infrastructure. Hardware-encrypted memory and hardware-based isolation help protect sensitive data while it is being processed. Workload attestation adds assurance before sensitive data or keys are released. For regulated, sensitive and mission-critical workloads, these safeguards provide another layer of protection while giving organizations greater control over where their data and applications run.

Azure Local will support multitenancy, allowing organizations to separate resources, governance and management across multiple tenants while sharing the underlying infrastructure. This significantly expands what customers with distinct business units or security boundaries can achieve with Sovereign Private Cloud. Multitenancy also creates new opportunities for local operators and service providers to deliver differentiated sovereign cloud services on Azure Local infrastructure.

These additions bring more of the application lifecycle under local control, spanning data, development, productivity, AI and operations. Organizations can determine what runs locally based on the requirements of each workload.

Extending the continuum through partners

Navigating sovereignty is increasingly complex. Regulatory, security, operational and business requirements vary across countries, industries and workloads. Organizations must translate these needs into technology and operating models that work in their local context. Meeting these needs often requires a combination of technology, local operating authority, sector expertise and specialized solutions.

The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the ways customers can address these requirements. National Partner Clouds, including Bleu in France, provide independently operated environments for customers that require a different ownership and operating model. Software partners can enhance Azure Local environments with capabilities across security, identity, observability, backup and recovery, migration, data, networking and applications. Digital sovereignty specialized partners combine Microsoft technologies with local knowledge and implementation expertise. Platform co-innovation partners expand infrastructure choice from datacenter to the edge.

This ecosystem gives customers the flexibility to combine technology, operating models and trusted expertise based on the requirements of each workload.

The next chapter of digital sovereignty

AI is amplifying both the opportunity and the impact of technology choices. As AI systems and agents interact with sensitive data, business processes and essential infrastructure, they also expand the security considerations organizations need to manage. Organizations need clear control over where these systems run, who can operate them, what actions they can take and how critical services continue when conditions change.

Microsoft Sovereign Cloud brings these choices together as a continuum of control across the public cloud, customer-operated environments and our partner ecosystem. It gives organizations the flexibility to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload while continuing to benefit from cloud capabilities and ongoing innovation.

We will continue to expand this continuum so organizations can innovate with cloud and AI while maintaining the control, confidentiality, resilience and operational authority their most important workloads require.
